https://www.baltictimes.com/pevkur__us_w.text: Estonia Latvia Lithuania Business Analysis Opinions Culture EU Affairs Search Archive Pevkur: US weapon shipments to reach Estonia in weeks, not months 2026-08-05 BNS/TBT Staff TALLINN – US arms deliveries, temporarily suspended due to the war in Ukraine, will reach Estonia in the coming weeks, with the exception of ATACMS missiles for HIMARS, which are currently unavailable from the Americans due to the war, Defense Minister Hanno Pevkur told public broadcaster ERR. Pevkur said in mid-July that an agreement had been reached with the Americans to resume arms deliveries and that all ordered ammunition had been cleared for shipment, except for ATACMS. At the time, he estimated that the various types of ammunition should arrive in Estonia in the coming months, with deliveries depending on logistical details. By the beginning of August, the timeline has shortened significantly, with delivery times now measured in weeks rather than months, Pevkur said on Wednesday. "In essence, the situation is the same; the movement of supplies is in progress, and to my knowledge, it's now a matter of weeks, not months. We do not want to disclose the exact delivery date for security reasons," he stated. However, tactical ATACMS missiles for the HIMARS multiple-launch rocket system, which have a range of up to 300 kilometers, are still unavailable from the Americans. The Estonian Defence Forces currently have six HIMARS (M142 High Mobility Artillery Rocket System) multiple-launch rocket systems. In April, the Estonian Centre for Defence Investments and the US defense company Lockheed Martin signed a contract to acquire three new HIMARS launchers, which are scheduled to arrive in Estonia in 2027, ERR reports. http://www.bgnes.com/politics/nato-holds.text: A multinational NATO exercise, “EAGLE SPEARHEAD,” is taking place in Romania, with today’s Distinguished Visitors Day at the “Getica” Training Center near Cincu, in Brașov County, drawing particular attention. The exercise is organized by NATO Battle Group Romania, with France serving as the framework nation. Around 1,000 troops from seven allied countries – Belgium, France, Italy, Luxembourg, Portugal, Spain and Romania – are taking part, Romania’s Ministry of National Defence said. As part of “EAGLE SPEARHEAD,” complex tactical drills are being conducted, including trench warfare operations and battlefield engineering. The exercise integrates various types of weapons and capabilities, including French Leclerc tanks and CAESAR self-propelled howitzers, Italian Ariete tanks, as well as reconnaissance and FPV drones. The main objective is to enhance the operational readiness and interoperability of allied formations and to test their ability to operate effectively in a multinational environment. The exercise is part of NATO’s preparations for deterrence and defence on the Alliance’s eastern and southeastern flanks. Bulgaria is not among the seven countries listed by Romania’s Ministry of National Defence as participating in “EAGLE SPEARHEAD” with military personnel. This means that Bulgaria is not directly contributing a contingent to the exercise. The exercise in Cincu is taking place against the backdrop of NATO’s increased military presence in Romania. The multinational battle group there is under French leadership and is a key element of the Alliance’s deterrence and defence posture in the Black Sea region. NATO says the formation has heavy armored vehicles, artillery, reconnaissance and mechanized infantry capabilities and can be reinforced with additional forces if necessary. | BGNES

https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/se.text: Passionate … The Last Bath View image in fullscreen Passionate … The Last Bath Movies Review The Last Bath review – self-mortifying nun struggles with profoundly uneasy sexual awakening Anabela Moreira is an impressively intense lead as the sister who finds herself in charge of her wayward teenage nephew Phil Hoad Mon 7 Sep 2026 08.00 EDT Last modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 08.03 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A sharp, self-abnegating performance from Anabela Moreira elevates this passionate – largely in the religious sense – Portuguese debut, which is only now arriving in the UK after festival screenings dating back to 2020. As senior nun Josefina, she wears a permanent cowl of careworn melancholy, suggesting a woman for whom, even after she is summoned to look after her bereaved 15-year-old nephew Alexandre (Martim Canavarro), holding the world at arm’s length is standard practice. Watching him slam into girl drivers on the fairground dodgems, it seems clear that desire is for other people. Or maybe not. Josefina is called back to her childhood village after the death of her father, who – in her wantaway sister’s absence – was Alexandre’s guardian. Traumatised by finding the body and spoiled because he was the first birth in the locality for years, the teenager requires mollycoddling. So Josefina finds herself in uncomfortable proximity to this coltish overgrown boy, who looks like a male model in waiting; bathing him, letting him sleep in her bed after he has wet his, inspecting his penis infection. She suffers it, presumably for love and our Lord. But when it becomes clear that he may be shipped off to a foster home if she doesn’t stick around, her inner motivations come into sharper focus. From the opening, symbolically charged image of Alexandre running haplessly around a maze of terraced vineyards, director David Bonneville has a keen sense of the higher implications of his story. He’s clearly interested in the boundaries and pathways behind spiritual, familial and physical love; finding a used condom in a bed at her convent, employing a self-mortifying garter, Josefina obviously regards the last of these as off-limits. But caring so intimately for Alexandre reawakens powerful feelings. The daily baths perhaps aren’t purely a devotional act; the photographs she takes of him sleeping testify to an adoration tipping into something transgressive. This growing possessiveness comes to a head with the return of Alexandre’s mother Angela (Margarida Moreira), a caricatured irresponsible glamourpuss who turns his head. The Last Bath’s resolution feels forced, which is a shame given the amount of faith Bonneville hitherto places in his audience in not giving them easy answers and letting this domestic mystery play breathe – a sign of the film’s spiritual strength. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqx2.text: Figure caption, Watch: "This is a war Europe is waging against us", Sergei Lavrov tells BBC By Steve Rosenberg Russia editor ,Â Reporting from Moscow Published 4 hours ago When Vladimir Putin arrived to address Russia's parliament on Wednesday, a warm welcome was guaranteed. "The Special Election Operation", as one Russian newspaper dubbed last month's legislative vote , has produced a State Duma even more pro-Putin than anything before it. The ruling party, United Russia, now has more MPs than ever. It allows the Kremlin to claim it has been handed a huge mandate from the Russian people. But for what? How will Putin use it? Are there any signs he is prepared to halt what he calls the special military operation? Or should we brace for further escalation in Ukraine and in tensions with Europe? On Thursday I'll be watching to see whether Russia's leader sheds light on his plans during an appearance at the Valdai Discussion Club in Moscow. Traditionally the president's speech at this annual foreign policy forum provides insight into Putin's world view. Right now, everything points to Putin continuing Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine: despite his country's huge battlefield losses to date and the damage being done to Russia's economy. Putin's speeches and statements suggest he remains confident that Russia can secure a military victory. Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, Russia's parliamentary vote in September was tightly controlled by the Kremlin and saw more United Russia MPs elected than ever before Judging by what is being reported in Russian media, Moscow is encouraged by the shortage of air defence missiles in Ukraine, as well as the expectation that Russian strikes this winter will increase pressure on Ukrainians. Kyiv has spoken of its difficulty in shooting down Russia's ballistic missiles and new jet-powered drones, which have been targeting Ukraine every day. And further afield? The Kremlin has made no secret of the fact it wants European states to slash their military and financial backing for Ukraine: the kind of support Moscow says is prolonging the war - or, rather, getting in the way of a Russian victory. To achieve this, Western officials believe Russia has been sending not so subtle signals. They accuse Moscow of waging an escalating hybrid war on European countries through cyber-attacks, acts of sabotage, and Russian drones violating European airspace. In Germany, a drone carrying an explosive device was found close to Ukrainian cargo planes at Leipzig airport. A covert campaign in the "grey zone", that space between peace and war. This week I asked Russia's foreign minister, Sergei Lavrov, does he admit that his country is waging a hybrid war against European countries? "Do you mean when we destroy drones and missiles that Britain and continental Europe are supplying Ukraine with, and which are used to attack us?" Lavrov replied. "If you admit your weapons are being used to strike us and we destroy them, call it whatever you want. But I have no doubt this is a war Europe is waging against us. We've been saying so for a long time." Image caption, "This is a war Europe is waging against us": Sergei Lavrov speaks to the BBC That, indeed, has been the official Russian stance for some time: that what is happening in Ukraine amounts to a European war on Russia. It is a narrative that skips over the fact that in 2022 it was the Kremlin that launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine, and that Russia continues to wage war there. How far would Russia go to sever European support for Kyiv? Is Moscow, for example, actively preparing to initiate military conflict in Europe with a Nato member state? That seems unlikely. After more than four-and-a-half years of war Russia's army has not yet managed to occupy the whole of Ukraine's eastern Donbas region, right next door to Russia. Fighting Europe may not be the plan, but freaking it out, to reduce support for Kyiv, could well be the intention. Listen to the messaging. "If they continue this war, a European war with American help, against Russia, on Ukrainian territory, sooner or later we'll feel the need to escalate," warns prominent foreign policy strategist Sergei Karaganov, honorary chairman of Russia's Council for Foreign and Defence Policy. "According to my scenarios, the first series of blows will be conventional," he told me. "But if Europe does not surrender, unfortunately, we will have to go nuclear. There will be little left of some European countries." But if Russia went nuclear there would be a response from Europe, and nothing would be left of Russia, I suggest. "No, there will be no response from Europe," said Karaganov. "What, Britain will attack Russia with nuclear weapons? I hope you're not that crazy. I'm sure the Americans are not that crazy." Image caption, Sergei Karaganov (R) says Russia will "have to go nuclear" if Europe keeps helping Ukraine I asked him if he agreed the last four-and-a-half years had been disastrous for Russia, in terms of casualties and the worsening security and economic situation. "We've lost a lot of people, yes," he admitted, "and I criticise my government for not being rough enough. But now we are getting rough enough in Ukraine. We're doing away with Ukraine as a viable state." If "doing away with Ukraine as a viable state" is Moscow's goal, it is hard to imagine the war ending soon. Meanwhile, Russia continues to rail against what it sees as the double standards of the West. In his recent address at the UN General Assembly, Sergei Lavrov accused the West of resorting to "brute force" around the world. "What they did in Venezuela, was that soft power or brute force?" Russia's foreign minister asked me this week. He was referring to America's military operation in Caracas to capture Venezuelan leader Nicolas Maduro back in January. "The fact that [the US] bombed and destroyed Iran's leadership, along with their families, including children, is that not brute force?" But was Russia not resorting to brute force every day in Ukraine, I replied. "If you mean the destruction of infrastructure used by a Nazi regime backed by the West to wage war on the Russian Federation, then we are resorting to brute force to eliminate this direct threat to us." Not only is this another element of Russia' official narrative: painting Ukraine as a neo-Nazi state, creating a false pretext to justify Russia's actions. With the admission of Russia's use of "brute force" in Ukraine, it is also further evidence that Moscow is in no mood to stop fighting. https://www.digi24.ro/stiri/externe/reac.text: Preşedintele Comisiei pentru informaţii a Senatului SUA, republicanul Tom Cotton, a declarat că negocierile cu Rusia pentru încetarea războiului în Ucraina nu au sens, deoarece cererile Kremlinului ca NATO să-şi retragă trupele la poziţiile din 1997, despre care au scris pe surse The New York Times şi alte publicaţii, demonstrează că Putin nu are de fapt intenţia de a ajunge la un acord de pace. „Retragerea ţărilor membre NATO din 'propriile lor' graniţe este o cerere absurdă din partea Rusiei. Putin a demonstrat încă o dată că nu este serios în privinţa unei păci negociate. În acest moment, continuarea discuţiilor nu este decât o farsă”, a scris senatorul republican pe X. În opinia sa, Putin va accepta să oprească războiul doar atunci când va conştientiza că nu poate câştiga. „Trebuie să ajutăm Ucraina să-i demonstreze acest lucru”, a adăugat Tom Cotton, potrivit News.ro. Senatorul - care tocmai a câştigat un nou mandat de şanse ani, al treilea, în alegerile recente din 3 noiembrie, fiind reales în Arkansas - a comentat un articol din The New York Times (NYT) potrivit căruia, în timpul negocierilor de la Abu Dhabi pentru încheierea războiului împotriva Ucrainei, Rusia a formulat din nou cererea ca NATO să-şi retragă trupele la poziţiile pe care Alianţa le ocupa în 1997. Cererea repetă, practic cuvânt cu cuvânt, poziţia Moscovei pe care aceasta o formulase cu două luni înainte de invazia pe scară largă a Ucrainei, la începutul anului 2022, când la Washington era în funcţie administraţia lui Joe Biden. Potrivit NYT, în cadrul negocierilor de la Abu Dhabi, ruşii au prezentat un document în care, printre altele, cereau ca NATO să-şi retragă trupele şi bazele la graniţele din 1997, precum şi să renunţe la extinderea în continuare a Alianţei şi la orice activitate militară în Europa de Est, în special în Ucraina. Poziţia fermă a Moscovei a fost prezentată într-un document pe care oficialii ruşi l-au distribuit săptămâna aceasta, conform unei copii primite de The New York Times de la o persoană implicată în negocieri. Documentul, a cărui autenticitate a fost confirmată de o altă persoană familiarizată cu desfăşurarea negocierilor, arată că liderul Federaţiei Ruse, Vladimir Putin , practic nu s-a abătut de la obiectivele sale principale după mai bine de 20 de luni de eforturi diplomatice ale administraţiei preşedintelui american Donald Trump. Documentul reia şi alte cerinţe ale Rusiei din decembrie 2021 (atunci Rusia solicita deja retragerea NATO la poziţiile din 1997) – renunţarea la extinderea în continuare a Alianţei şi la „orice activitate militară” în Ucraina şi în alte regiuni, în special în Europa de Est, în Caucazul de Sud şi în Asia Centrală. În plus, Rusia doreşte ca Franţa şi Marea Britanie să renunţe la utilizarea armelor nucleare pentru apărarea altor ţări europene. De asemenea, documentul menţionează încetarea ajutorului acordat Ucrainei. În schimb, Federaţia Rusă este dispusă să aprobe aderarea Ucrainei la Uniunea Europeană, dar numai cu condiţia ca ucrainenii să nu participe la politica comună de apărare a blocului european. După cum subliniază NYT, oficialii ruşi au arătat clar la Abu Dhabi că ruşii privesc în continuare Războiul Rece şi Blocul de la Varşovia condus de Uniunea Sovietică (în conformitate cu Tratatul de la Varşovia din 1955) drept un model pentru Europa postbelică actuală. În acelaşi timp, potrivit unei surse a NYT, emisarii speciali ai preşedintelui SUA, Steve Witkoff şi Jared Kushner, le-au transmis reprezentanţilor ruşi că, de la sfârşitul anului 2021, multe lucruri s-au schimbat şi i-au îndemnat să „privească spre viitor”. Cu toate acestea, în cadrul întâlnirii cu Putin de la Moscova, unde Witkoff şi Kushner s-au deplasat după încheierea negocierilor de la Abu Dhabi, liderul Kremlinului le-a spus americanilor că cererea Rusiei din 2021 privind retragerea trupelor NATO la poziţiile din 1997 reflectă în continuare „viziunea Rusiei asupra pilonilor arhitecturii de securitate”. Recent, publicaţia britanică The Telegraph, citând surse din cercurile diplomatice, a scris că Rusia ar putea încerca să profite de o nouă rundă de negocieri de pace pentru a obţine concesii din partea NATO. În plus, pe fondul negocierilor privind încetarea războiului din Ucraina, Ministerul Afacerilor Externe al Rusiei a propus ideea unei noi arhitecturi de securitate a Europei, care prevede încheierea unor acorduri bilaterale de neagresiune cu unele state membre ale NATO. Pe de altă parte, sâmbătă, preşedintele Volodimir Zelenski a declarat că Statele Unite i-au propus să cedeze teritorii în schimbul aderării Ucrainei la NATO, iar Kievul se află în negocieri privind garanţii de securitate „specifice” din partea Occidentului, liderul ucrainean asigurând că va solicita aprobarea compatrioţilor săi în cazul în care s-ar încheia un acord. Şi tabloidul german BILD a scris despre cereri care ar face parte dintr-una dintre propunerile Rusiei privind o „nouă ordine de securitate europeană”. Publicaţia subliniază însă că aceasta este doar una dintre numeroasele propuneri discutate prin canale neoficiale de negociere. Potrivit acestor condiţii, ambiţiile Kremlinului se extind asupra mai multor ţări, nu numai asupra Ucrainei. Astfel, Finlanda ar trebui să părăsească NATO, iar Alianţei i s-ar interzice să menţină baze militare în Estonia, Letonia şi Lituania. Mai mult, cererile s-ar referi inclusiv la Republica Moldova. Moscova reia ideea mai veche de transformare a ţării într-o federaţie care să includă Găgăuzia şi Transnistria. Aceste regiuni ar avea dreptul să organizeze referendumuri de independenţă în cazul în care Moldova ar adera la UE. La schimb, Rusia propune retragerea armelor sale nucleare din Belarus, abţinerea de la desfăşurarea de rachete cu rază intermediară de acţiune în această ţară şi retragerea trupelor ruse din Transnistria, a scris BILD.
